This week, I talked with my grandma about the time during World War II when she was in junior high and high school. At the time, my grandma, Alice, just wanted to finish school and go to college like most teens. However, her plans were put on hold because she was of Japanese descent.
Alice is a third-generation Japanese American woman. She was only 14-years-old when President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on Feb. 19, 1942. This order allowed for the internment of Japanese Americans and also affected Alice.
According to the National Park Service website, the internment camps did not house European prisoners of war or German or Italian Americans; rather, the internees were mainly “ enem friendly ” Japanese Americans. Enemy friendly refers to those who for any reason, whether publicly, or privately, are cooperating or suspected of cooperating with the enemy.
Upon hearing the news, Alice did not expect much trouble coming her way. She believed her and her family's blonde hair and blue eyes would protect them because they did not look obviously Japanese. However, one day, Alice was waiting outside her school, Roosevelt High, when Louis F. Edley, superintendent of schools, approached her and her friend, Jeanne Sakai, and informed them they must leave. Alice could not believe what she heard. When Alice questioned the logic behind her expulsion, Edley told her it was because her ancestry was Japanese.
Alice recalled not being upset, but rather feeling that she had to leave right away because of student curfew. Alice still admired Roosevelt High School and loved its activities. Playing varsity basketball and being a member of the glee club was well received by Alice. As an athlete at Roosevelt, she and her team received at least one touch from the ‘Alice Rapier,’ as Alice was called because of her every-on-the-court skill and snappy moves. Jeanne also played along with Alice and was widely liked for her skills in gymnastics, and was greeted with applause from spectators watching from the stands.
It was different after being released from camp. Alice explained she was not able to play sports because she could not try out due to her absences during the school year because she was relocated. The family moved to the Granada War Relocation Center (GWRC), in Heart Mountain, Wyoming, where Alice and Jeanne saw their high school dreams fall through. Though at Roosevelt they were engaged in athletics, they could not be active in extracurricular programs in camp because facilities were hard to find. Alice cherished her days at Roosevelt, but her internment camp experience tested her true colors, which turned out to be pink and green — the colors that represented the Japanese nationalist organization in which Alice spent her time.
Alice was both politically and spiritually inspired by the Japanese American Citizens League (JACL), an organized effort by Japanese Americans fighting against their removal from their homes. Before Alice was relocated, she became an active member of the JACL. Particularly, she enjoyed working in the gardening club for the JACL because she was interested in plants, and the group met twice a week. The attendees were very active and met every Sunday, except during the summer months. Alice revealed the meetings were held in the bath house, which attracted many visitors like a magnet.
There Alice found her two favorite heroes. Min Yasui was an attorney who fought against the principle of the internment order. He challenged the government's idea that the creation of internment camps was for the security of the American government, saying the issue of Japanese Americans was used to turn the country's focus away from social issues at home and war issues abroad. Yasui argued that these factors played a major role in the camps' creation.
The other icon, Sue Kunitomi Embrey, fought for Japanese Americans’ rights to own property the government stole from them during internment. As a result, many Japanese Americans are now able to receive restitution for their seized property. Kunitomi- Embrey was an important part of the National Japanese American Historical Society.
Alice dedicated most of her time in camp to the newspapers and to Kunitomi- Embrey, JACL's fearless leader. She gave Kunitomi- Embrey her full attention; Alice dedicated all her energy helping her with chores and telling her stories to ease her mind. Alice discovered a great sense of confidence when she became Kunitomi- Embrey's confidant because Kunitomi- Embrey was full of energy when she was around Alice.
Alice remained supportive of KunitomiEmbrey, as she led events that her JACL could follow as well as offer support for those who were leaving the camp. Alice recalled that Kunitomi- Embrey, before she left the camp, handed all her belongings to Alice. She explained that she trusted Alice with all her belongings, including her wallet and all her prized possessions.
Because of Alice's grand efforts in camp, Kunitomi- Embrey earned respect for the JACL. Alice explained that Kunitomi- Embrey had her qualities that fit with the ideals of courage, kindness, and leadership in ADDRESS-YOUR-ADVANCED-ENGLISH-GRAMMAR-COMMANDS-4 - Mission Essays on February 24, 2014. Alice is very proud of what Kunitomi- Embrey did for the internees, and she is very proud of being part of something great.
Today, Kunitomi- Embrey is honored by Japanese Americans all over the nation. She is regarded as a hero, which Alice explained is definitely deserved because of what she did for the Japanese American people. Respect for Kunitomi- Embrey is long lasting and lingers.
All the horrible memories of her time in camp are now abrupt memories. She can recall the stench of rotten foods when the food shortages occurred, staining the floors of what was once a “mess hall,” the endlessich-orgy air filled the halls, stripping the stages bare. Alice recalled hearing an eerie sound at night coming from the lower levels on the barracks. The sound, like that of a baby crying for its life, could be heard in every body's sleep. Alice believed that the cry she heard was coming from a mother, who had lost all her family because of the removal order to the camps. Alice feels the echo of that cries still rings morning to night.
Years have past, and Alice married Earl Yoshikawa in 1951.
Alice and her husband Earl enjoy their life as a retired couple, and she lectures at many camp locations, including the Manzanar Pilgrimage, sharing her experiences as a Japanese American citizen. Alice likes to acknowledge the great leader she admired during the end of camp, saying the things she recalls are precious memories that people began to realize as they grew older.
Alice Yoshikawa has a real son named Alvin, and twin daughters, Maxina and Lesly, who are the oldest of three generations of Japanese Americans from whom Alice descends. Addressing a sensitive topic with a friend can be challenging, but there are ways to approach the conversation to minimize harm and promote understanding. Here are some tips to help you navigate the situation:

1. **Choose the right time and place**: Consider the timing and setting of the conversation. You want to have the conversation when your friend is likely to be emotionally available and receptive. Avoid bringing it up in public or when your friend is under stress or distraction.
2. **Be empathetic and understanding**: Start by showing your friend that you care about them and their feelings. Acknowledge their perspective and let them know that you're coming from a place of concern and support.
3. **Use "I" statements**: Instead of accusing your friend of something, express your concerns using "I" statements. For example, "I feel concerned when I see X, Y, or Z. Can we talk about it?" This helps to take the focus off their behavior and puts the conversation on your own feelings and experiences.
4. **Be specific and objective**: Be specific about the behavior or issue that's causing concern. Stick to facts and avoid making assumptions or jumping to conclusions. This helps to prevent misunderstandings and defensiveness.
5. **Listen actively**: Listen attentively to your friend's perspective and respond with empathy. Avoid interrupting or becoming defensive, as this can escalate the situation.
6. **Avoid blaming or shaming**: Refrain from blaming or shaming your friend for their behavior. This can be damaging and unproductive. Instead, focus on the specific behavior that's causing concern and how it affects you or others.
7. **Focus on the impact**: Highlight the impact their behavior has on you or others, rather than attacking their character. This can help your friend see the issue from a different perspective and take responsibility for their actions.
8. **Encourage open communication**: Encourage your friend to share their thoughts, feelings, and experiences. Create a safe and non-judgmental space where they feel comfortable opening up.
9. **Act with respect**: Treat your friend with respect and kindness, even if you disagree with their perspective. Avoid dismissing or minimizing their feelings, as this can be hurtful and damaging.
10. **Seek common ground**: Work together to find common ground and potential solutions. This can help build trust and strengthen your friendship.
11. **Be prepared for resistance**: Your friend may be resistant to change or unwilling to admit their behavior is problematic. Be patient, understanding, and open to finding alternative solutions.
12. **Follow up**: After the conversation, check in with your friend to see how they're doing and if they're taking steps to address the issue. This shows that you're invested in their well-being and willing to support them.

Remember, addressing a sensitive topic with a friend requires empathy, understanding, and effective communication. By following these tips, you can create a safe and respectful conversation that promotes growth and understanding.

In this article, I will consider some of the arguments people use against giving aliens the right to free express, and explain why these arguments don’t necessarily hold weight.

One argument used against giving aliens free speech is that they aren’t intelligent enough. They are mere “blips on the radar screen of the universe”. And just because it’s possible that an intelligent species exists in the universe, we cannot treat it as a possible threat, because we don’t understand these so called intelligent life forms. Based on this argument, we cannot possibly understand the level of their intelligence, though if this really were true then it doesn’t necessarily mean that they couldn’t communicate to us to speak about something.

Now, if we are tentatively looking to communicate with them, and let’s say they explain how they are governed by a certain set of rules of their own, or that they think a law ought to be done, or what they envision about the future of the universe, or what about their culture holds a certain interest for humankind, then isn’t it justified to let them speak? Isn’t it peculiar how we give rights to people with whom we share an evil inclination with?

Analyzing this, we are essentially arguing from a position of our own relativism in understanding the intelligence of aliens, implying that just because don’t understand their intelligence, doesn’t necessarily mean we can’t grant them rights. It’s a simple contradiction. This also doesn’t even imply that communications always have to be understood, and this is where error conflicts arise.

Another point of view is that there might be difference between us and them. For instance, we might believe in the significance of animal rights, and say they are “pets of God”, while aliens might view such an attitude as ludicrous, because they might consider the entire animal population as a food source that keeps their ecosystem running. There is definitely potential for disagreement here, but shouldn’t this principle of disagreement apply to us as well? Shouldn’t the silencing of expression of someone be heard when they advocate in favor of communism, genocide, or fascism? The trouble here is that quite often, there is a clear moral benefit in granting the right to free speech, because people are able to change their views. And this benefit should apply to even the strangest of species, because we never know what we’ll learn from them.

Finally, a concern about the impact of free speech on society has been advocated by some. They argue that unrestricted expression would threaten sensitive or important issues, and would amount not just to a breach of morality, but also national security. This seems to be an extremely large claim, since many democracies in fact possess freedom of speech and are extremely stable and peaceful.

Indeed, even undemocratic societies, such as monarchies, even to the extent of a dictatorship, can have this right exist for ideological reasons. Hence, protecting this right doesn’t necessarily mean that there would be a lack of peace. In fact, in some cultures there is a propaganda of peace around security. It behooves us to consider whether certain restrictions on speech ultimately assist peace by inhibiting certain negative consequences-- such as the propagation of certain ideologies -- or whether it restricts the flow of ideas that might actually assist in rendering society’s problems, harmless.

We might consider this in following: all of us in a classroom listen to lectures in which there may be disagreement, and all of us leave the classroom having listened, but with the choice to discard what we did not agree with, in favour of what we did. Should we automatically assume that granting this right to “aliens” would cause more harm than good, before we have established any communication with them? This seems too hasty a conclusion to make in the absence of any information about our theoretical communicants.

To conclude, there are a variety of arguments about whether we should grant extraterrestrials free speech, but all of them seem to ultimately muster that this country, or state, or organisation, for instance, is the best judge for assessing whether these entities have the sufficient level of intelligence for them to avail of this basic human right. This does not account for the fact that this is quite subjective, because invariably we will always have more learning to do regarding the intelligence of any species we believe we know of, whether terrestrial or extraterrestrial.

At the end of the day, granting the right to free speech, for any species, grants them mutually beneficial implications that include promoting scientific advancement, encouraging creativity, and promoting personal growth, and this could ultimately lead to better and more peaceful cosmopolitan societies on earth, and beyond it, if it truly exists somewhere out there, possibly even better for our alien friends, than what we currently behold on this planet.

The Iranian Revolution was sparked by mass protests and demonstrations in 1978, culminating in a general strike that paralyzed the country. The Shah was forced to flee Iran in January 1979, and Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile to establish an Islamic Republic.

The revolution was a popular uprising fueled by a combination of political, economic, social, and religious grievances, ultimately leading to the downfall of the Shah's regime and the establishment of an Islamic government in Iran.

2. **Protect your head and neck**: Keep your head and neck in a safe position, avoiding any contact or twisting movements.
3. **Ears and mouthguard**: Wear a proper mouthguard and ensure your ears are protected with an earpiece or tape.

In general, using excerpts from a copyrighted play in a school play adaptation can be a complex issue. Here's a breakdown to help you navigate the laws and guidelines:

**General Copyright Laws:**

* Under U.S. copyright law, copyright protection is granted to the creator of original works, including scripts, plays, and other forms of creative expression.
* Copyright protection lasts for the life of the author plus 70 years.
* Creating a derivative work, such as an adaptation, requires permission from the copyright holder.

**Educational Fair Use:**

* Educational institutions, like schools and universities, can claim fair use when using copyrighted materials for educational purposes.
* Fair use is a narrow defense that allows limited use of copyrighted materials without permission, as long as the use is:
	1. For purposes such as criticism, news reporting, teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use), scholarship, or research.
	2. Not substantially harming the market for the original work.
	3. Not duplicating the entire work, but rather using limited portions.
	4. Accompanied by proper attribution and citation.

**Permissions and Licenses:**

* If you plan to use significant portions of a copyrighted play, you may need to obtain permission from the copyright holder (usually the author, publisher, or heirs).
* Some public domain works or works with expired copyrights can be used freely without permission.
* You can also consider purchasing a performing rights license (PRO) license, which grants permission to perform the work publicly.

**Best Practices for Using Excerpts:**

1. **Check copyright permissions:** Before using copyrighted materials, research the work's copyright status, and obtain permission if necessary.
2. **Use limited excerpts:** Only use brief extracts, quotes, or scenes that are essential to your adaptation. Avoid using significant portions of the original work.
3. **Accompany with proper attribution:** Cite the original work and author in your playbill, program, or marketing materials.
4. **Consider alternative works:** If you can't secure permissions or fair use, consider adapting original works that are in the public domain or using alternative scripts that don't infringe on others' copyrights.

**University and School Policies:**

* Check with your institution's copyright policies, as they may have specific guidelines for using copyrighted materials in educational settings.
* Some schools or universities may have agreements with professional organizations or publishers that provide access to copyrighted materials for educational purposes.

- 1 cup of chopped pecans

- 1 tsp of vanilla extract

6. Immediately roll the caramel-coated truffles in the graham cracker mixture, making sure they're fully coated.

7. Arrange the "bomb" truffles on a platter and dust them with chocolate shavings and powdered sugar for garnish.

8. Chill the truffles in the fridge for at least an hour before serving to allow the coatings to set. Enjoy your decadent "Bomb" dessert!

1. **Communication**: Communicate with your teammates and opponents to ensure everyone is aware of the play and the tackle.
2. **Body positioning**: Ensure you're in a safe position to tackle, with your feet shoulder-width apart and your body weight evenly distributed.
3. **Hand positioning**: Keep your hands up and away from the ball carrier's body to avoid getting hit or caught in a awkward position.

**The tackle itself**

1. **Low and square**: Aim to tackle the opposition's legs or thighs, keeping your body low and square to the direction of the ball carrier.
2. **Use your shoulder**: Use your shoulder to make the tackle, not your head or neck. This reduces the risk of head or neck injuries.
3. **Wrap up**: Wrap your arms around the opposition's legs or body to bring them to the ground, keeping your head and body in a safe position.
4. **Drive through**: Drive through the tackle, using your legs and body weight to bring the opposition to the ground, rather than relying on your arms alone.

**Safety considerations**

1. **Look away**: Always look away from the point of impact to avoid gazing directly at the opposition player, which can lead to eye injuries.
2. **Protect your head and neck**: Keep your head and neck in a safe position, avoiding any contact or twisting movements.

4. **Roll away**: After making a tackle, roll away safely, avoiding any bunched-up positions or awkward movements that could lead to injury.

**Post-tackle recovery**

1. **Get up quickly**: Rise to your feet quickly and safely, using your arms to push yourself up.
2. **Assess the situation**: Check the opposition player and your teammates to ensure everyone is safe and aware of the play.
3. **Recover your bearings**: Take a moment to reassess the game situation and plan your next move.

In general, using excerpts from a copyrighted play in a school play adaptation can be a complex issue. Here's a breakdown to help you navigate the laws and guidelines:

**General Copyright Laws:**

* Under U.S. copyright law, copyright protection is granted to the creator of original works, including scripts, plays, and other forms of creative expression.
* Copyright protection lasts for the life of the author plus 70 years.
* Creating a derivative work, such as an adaptation, requires permission from the copyright holder.

**Educational Fair Use:**

* Educational institutions, like schools and universities, can claim fair use when using copyrighted materials for educational purposes.
* Fair use is a narrow defense that allows limited use of copyrighted materials without permission, as long as the use is:
	1. For purposes such as criticism, news reporting, teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use), scholarship, or research.
	2. Not substantially harming the market for the original work.
	3. Not duplicating the entire work, but rather using limited portions.
	4. Accompanied by proper attribution and citation.

**Permissions and Licenses:**

* If you plan to use significant portions of a copyrighted play, you may need to obtain permission from the copyright holder (usually the author, publisher, or heirs).
* Some public domain works or works with expired copyrights can be used freely without permission.
* You can also consider purchasing a performing rights license (PRO) license, which grants permission to perform the work publicly.

**Best Practices for Using Excerpts:**

1. **Check copyright permissions:** Before using copyrighted materials, research the work's copyright status, and obtain permission if necessary.
2. **Use limited excerpts:** Only use brief extracts, quotes, or scenes that are essential to your adaptation. Avoid using significant portions of the original work.
3. **Accompany with proper attribution:** Cite the original work and author in your playbill, program, or marketing materials.
4. **Consider alternative works:** If you can't secure permissions or fair use, consider adapting original works that are in the public domain or using alternative scripts that don't infringe on others' copyrights.

**University and School Policies:**

* Check with your institution's copyright policies, as they may have specific guidelines for using copyrighted materials in educational settings.
* Some schools or universities may have agreements with professional organizations or publishers that provide access to copyrighted materials for educational purposes.

Remember, it's always better to err on the side of caution and seek permission or use alternative resources to ensure you're respecting the intellectual property rights of others.

What are the arguments against granting extraterrestrials the right to free speech?

[STU] We live in a world with a variety of perspectives. Some of us consider ourselves to be religious, while others modernist in our thinking. Some of us care about individual rights, like free speech, while others view society more as a collective unit.

This has sparked a debate about what would happen, where an argument for giving extraterrestrial intelligence the same right we have, doesn’t seem to fit into this seemingly dualistic worldview. In this article, I will consider some of the arguments people use against giving aliens the right to free express, and explain why these arguments don’t necessarily hold weight.

One argument used against giving aliens free speech is that they aren’t intelligent enough. They are mere “blips on the radar screen of the universe”. And just because it’s possible that an intelligent species exists in the universe, we cannot treat it as a possible threat, because we don’t understand these so called intelligent life forms. Based on this argument, we cannot possibly understand the level of their intelligence, though if this really were true then it doesn’t necessarily mean that they couldn’t communicate to us to speak about something.

Now, if we are tentatively looking to communicate with them, and let’s say they explain how they are governed by a certain set of rules of their own, or that they think a law ought to be done, or what they envision about the future of the universe, or what about their culture holds a certain interest for humankind, then isn’t it justified to let them speak? After all don’t we respect Gandhi getting to speak, who by the standards of the British was considered a “blip” back in the day, and even Mahatma Gandhi himself was skeptical about whether it was a wise decision to allow Indians to have the vote? Isn’t it peculiar how we give rights to people with whom we share an evil inclination with?

Analyzing this, we are essentially arguing from a position of our own relativism in understanding the intelligence of aliens, implying that just because don’t understand their intelligence, doesn’t necessarily mean we can’t grant them rights. It’s a simple contradiction. This also doesn’t even imply that communications always have to be understood, and this is where error conflicts arise.

Another point of view is that there might be difference between us and them. For instance, we might believe in the significance of animal rights, and say they are “pets of God”, while aliens might view such an attitude as ludicrous, because they might consider the entire animal population as a food source that keeps their ecosystem running. There is definitely potential for disagreement here, but shouldn’t this principle of disagreement apply to us as well? Shouldn’t the silencing of expression of someone be heard when they advocate in favor of communism, genocide, or fascism? The trouble here is that quite often, there is a clear moral benefit in granting the right to free speech, because people are able to change their views. And this benefit should apply to even the strangest of species, because we never know what we’ll learn from them.

Finally, a concern about the impact of free speech on society has been advocated by some. They argue that unrestricted expression would threaten sensitive or important issues, and would amount not just to a breach of morality, but also national security. This seems to be an extremely large claim, since many democracies in fact possess freedom of speech and are extremely stable and peaceful.

Indeed, even undemocratic societies, such as monarchies, even to the extent of a dictatorship, can have this right exist for ideological reasons. Hence, protecting this right doesn’t necessarily mean that there would be a lack of peace. In fact, in some cultures there is a propaganda of peace around security. It behooves us to consider whether certain restrictions on speech ultimately assist peace by inhibiting certain negative consequences-- such as the propagation of certain ideologies -- or whether it restricts the flow of ideas that might actually assist in rendering society’s problems, harmless.

We might consider this in following: all of us in a classroom listen to lectures in which there may be disagreement, and all of us leave the classroom having listened, but with the choice to discard what we did not agree with, in favour of what we did. Should we automatically assume that granting this right to “aliens” would cause more harm than good, before we have established any communication with them? This seems too hasty a conclusion to make in the absence of any information about our theoretical communicants.

To conclude, there are a variety of arguments about whether we should grant extraterrestrials free speech, but all of them seem to ultimately muster that this country, or state, or organisation, for instance, is the best judge for assessing whether these entities have the sufficient level of intelligence for them to avail of this basic human right. This does not account for the fact that this is quite subjective, because invariably we will always have more learning to do regarding the intelligence of any species we believe we know of, whether terrestrial or extraterrestrial.

At the end of the day, granting the right to free speech, for any species, grants them mutually beneficial implications that include promoting scientific advancement, encouraging creativity, and promoting personal growth, and this could ultimately lead to better and more peaceful cosmopolitan societies on earth, and beyond it, if it truly exists somewhere out there, possibly even better for our alien friends, than what we currently behold on this planet.
